newsitem.title: LATVIA: Baltic premiers vow to stamp out money laundering.
newsitem.headline: Baltic premiers vow to stamp out money laundering.

text.p: The prime ministers of the Baltic states of Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania vowed on Thursday to step up their fight against the money laundering and organised crime rife in the region after the fall of the Soviet Union.
The three small countries have become key transit points for criminal gangs, which have flourished amid the economic chaos that accompanied the collapse of the Soviet empire.
Since Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia regained their independence in 1991, nuclear materials, big groups of illegal immigrants and drugs have all been seized on their soil.
Money laundering in their infant and badly regulated financial systems has also become a growing problem.

Latvian Prime Minister Andris Shkele, Estonian premier Tiit Vaehi and Lithuania's Mindaugas Stankevicius signed a declaration at a conference on money laundering sponsored by the United Nations Drug Control Programme (UNDCP).

"We, on behalf of the governments of Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, reaffirm our commitment to prevent by any and all means the use of our countries' finanical institutions for the purpose of laundering criminal proceeds," the declaration said.
The three leaders said they would enact new laws to bring their countries into line with European Union (EU) standards, tighten existing rules and set up special supervisory bodies.
Experts at the conference could not say how much money is laundered in the Baltic states but put the worldwide sum at $300 billion to $500 billion annually.
A lot of the cash laundered in the Baltics is believed to be done by criminal gangs operating mainly in Russia but who use the Baltic countries as offshore money centres.
